To measure the forgetting quality and predictive perfor- mance of the model after the unlearning process (i.e., un- learning model), several unlearning metrics have been pro- posed (Kashef, 2021; Shokri et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021; Brophy & Lowd, 2021; Cao & Yang, 2015). However, ex- isting unlearning metrics, such as unlearning accuracy (UA) (Brophy & Lowd, 2021; Foster et al., 2024) and member- ship inference attack (MIA) (Shokri et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021), fall short in fully evaluating forgetting quality and reliability. These metrics primarily focus on whether mod- els can predict forget data accurately without sufficiently addressing how well the model forgets. In a nutshell, mis- classifying forget data does not mean that the model has completely forgotten it to some extent. 1 arXiv:2501.19403v1 [cs.LG] 31 Jan 2025 Conformal Prediction-Motivated Machine Unlearning To verify this view, we apply conformal prediction (Pa- padopoulos et al., 2002; Lei & Wasserman, 2014) to the unlearning models. Through experiments, we find that al- though the model misclassifies some forget data, a signifi- cant portion of these misclassified instances still appear in the conformal prediction set. Pictures in Table 1, which visu- alize the important feature of models’ prediction of models by using Grad-CAM (Selvaraju et al., 2017), further explain this phenomenon. Despite the Finetune method incorrectly predicting the forget data, the Grad-CAM maps still focus heavily on the important features of the object itself. Based on the above findings, we design two novel metrics that capture the uncertainty and robustness of unlearning performance more effectively inspired by conformal predic- tion. Additionally, motivated by Carlini & Wagner (C&W) attack (Carlini & Wagner, 2017) and conformal prediction, we propose a general unlearning framework to improve training-based unlearning methods and promote reliable for- getting. Grad-CAM maps of our method in Table 1 reveal that once the true label no longer falls within the conformal prediction set, the activation regions shift significantly. To sum up, the contributions of our work are as follows: • We identify pivotal limitations in current unlearning metrics, as they overlook misclassified data where ground truth labels remain potential candidates under uncertainty quantification. • We design two novel metrics to address the limitations motivated by conformal prediction. • We propose a general unlearning framework for training-based machine unlearning methods motivated by conformal prediction and C&W loss. • Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of novel metrics and our unlearning framework. 2. Enhancing Metrics for Machine Unlearning Based on Conformal Prediction 2.1. Preliminaries and Notations Machine Unlearning. Machine unlearning is the targeted removal of certain training data effects from a machine learn- ing model. In our work, two different forgetting scenarios are considered: (i) random data forgetting focuses on ran- domly forgetting specific instances within the training data, and (ii) class-wise forgetting aims to remove all information associated with an entire class. Let Dtrain denote the orig- inal training data used to obtain an original model θo. We split the whole training data Dtrain into two subsets, forget data Df and retain data Dr = Dtrain \ Df. In random data forgetting, Dtest represents test data. In class-wise forgetting, Dtf corresponds to the test-forget data, exclu- sively containing the forget class, while Dtr represents the test-retain data within the test data Dtest. Let θu denote the model after the unlearning process, where the influence of forget data Df has been removed. The purpose of machine unlearning is to enable θu to forget Df (thus no longer rec- ognizing Dtf in the class-wise forgetting scenario), while maintaining accuracy on the retain data Dr and avoiding a significant drop in accuracy on Dtest in the random data forgetting scenario or Dtr in the class-wise setting. Conformal Prediction. Conformal prediction is proposed to quantify uncertainty in machine learning models, provid- ing prediction sets that contain the true label with a guaran- teed probability (Angelopoulos & Bates, 2021). Among the various types of conformal prediction, this work specifically focuses on split conformal prediction (SCP)1. To construct the conformal prediction set, it involves four steps: 1. Calibration Data. SCP first chooses unseen data as calibration data. The number of calibration data points should be enough to evaluate the model’s uncertainty. 2. Non-conformity Score. In our work, we follow the conventional choice and set the non-conformity score as S(x, yi) = 1 −pi(x), (1) where pi(x) represents the probability output (through a softmax function) for the class yi. 3. Quantile Computation. Given a target miscoverage rate α ∈[0, 1], SCP obtains threshold ˆq by taking the 1−α quantile of the non-conformity score on the calibration data Dc. 4. Prediction Set. For the data point x that needs to be tested, labels with non-conformity scores lower than the threshold ˆq are selected for the final prediction set: C(x) = {yi : S(x, yi) ≤ˆq}, (2) where yi represents different classes. 2.2. We apply the most commonly used metrics, unlearning ac- curacy (UA), retain accuracy (RA), test accuracy (TA) and MIA, to evaluate three classic machine unlearning methods: Retrain (RT), Finetune (FT) (Warnecke et al., 2021), and Random Label (RL) (Graves et al., 2021). These methods are implemented on a ResNet-18 model trained with the CIFAR-10 dataset in a random data forgetting scenario. In Table 2, compared with RA on Dr, the UA of the three meth- ods proves that the model indeed forgets some forget data. The MIA column also indicates that many data points seem to be forgotten. These metrics appear to provide valuable insights into the extent of forgetting achieved. However, higher unlearning accuracy cannot ensure that these forget data points are no longer represented in any form within the model’s predictions. To validate our hypothesis, we employ the process of con- formal prediction to examine whether the true labels of the forget data appear within the prediction set. We set the con- fidence level to 95%, i.e., α = 0.05, and set the calibration set size to 2, 000. In Table 3, we count both UA metric and MIA metric’s misclassified data points (mis-label) and, after applying conformal prediction, determined how many of these points fall within the conformal prediction set (in-set). Table 3 demonstrates that even though the model misclas- sifies part of the forget data, on average 54.6% of these misclassified instances are still present in the conformal prediction set. This indicates that a high UA does not mean the model has truly forgotten the data. Relying solely on UA to evaluate the forgetting quality is insufficient. In MIA, the prediction of ‘0’ indicates a data point is pre- dicted as “truly forget”, while ‘1’ signifies “still retain”. And “mis-label” refers to the number of the model predicts the forget data points as ‘0’. In conformal prediction of MIA, there are three potential prediction set results, i.e., {0}, {1}, {0, 1}. The “in-set” here refers to the number of mislabeled data points whose conformal prediction set in- cludes 1. Thus, the in-set ratio indicates that, although the MIA fails to identify an average of 18.33% of the forget data points, conformal prediction can still recognize more than half of these forget data points within its prediction set. Overall, high in-set ratios in conformal prediction highlight that a considerable portion of the forget data remains iden- tifiable through conformal prediction. This implies these unlearning methods may not be fully effective in eliminating traces of the forget data from another perspective. 2.3. Designing Metrics Motivated by Conformal Prediction Based on the limitations of UA and MIA metrics shown in Section 2.2, it raises a question as follows: (Q2) Can we develop metrics to address the short- comings of UA and MIA? Thus, we propose enhanced UA and MIA metrics that draw intuition from conformal prediction. 2.3.1. DEFINITION OF NEW METRICS Conformal Ratio (CR). To overcome the limitations of UA, we introduce a novel metric, Conformal Ratio (CR), which incorporates both coverage and set size in confor- mal prediction to provide a more comprehensive evaluation. Before defining CR, we introduce Coverage and Set Size. The definition of Coverage, given a dataset D, is as follows: Coverage := 1 |D| X (x,yt)∈D I(yt ∈C(x)), (3) where yt is the true label of data point x. Coverage reflects the probability that the true label falls within the prediction set C(x). For D = Df, high coverage indicates that the model retains significant information about forget data, sug- gesting incomplete unlearning. Conversely, higher coverage is better for test data Dtest. 3 Conformal Prediction-Motivated Machine Unlearning Given a dataset D, Set Size can be defined as follows: Set Size := 1 |D| X (x,yt)∈D |C(x)|, (4) where |C(x)| represents the prediction set size of a specific instance. When D = Df, a smaller set size implies that the model cannot forget specific information about Df well. In contrast, when D = Dtest, a small set size may indicate that the model maintains a strong performance after unlearning. Based on Coverage and Set Size, we introduce the definition of CR for a dataset D as follows: CR := Coverage Set Size = P (x,yt)∈D I(yt ∈C(x)) P (x,yt)∈D |C(x)| . (5) CR balances the information captured by coverage and set size. A lower CR value implies successful unlearning on forget data Df, but a significant drop in the model’s utility for Dtest. CR is inspired by conformal prediction which is proposed to assess the model’s behavior on new, unseen data (e.g., validation or test data), not on the training data. Thus, we emphasize that CR only measures forget data Df and test data Dtest. MIA Conformal Ratio (MIACR). To address the limita- tions of the current MIA metric, we propose a new metric called MIACR. For three potential prediction sets {0}, {1} and {0, 1}, set {0} is the only ideal case for MIA prediction since ‘1’ represents the data point is part of the training data. Therefore, we introduce a new metric to measure the probability of the set {0} occurring, referred to as MIACR: MIACR := 1 |Df| X (x,yt)∈Df I(C(x) = {0}), (6) where C(x) = {0} denotes prediction set is {0}. MIACR only calculates the average of C(x) = {0}, and a higher MIACR value represents better forgetting for Df. Superiority of Our Metrics. Unlike existing metrics, both the CR and MIACR metrics incorporate the fact that the true labels of some forgotten data points may remain within the prediction set, even when the predictions deviate from the true labels. This allows for a more robust assessment of the model’s forgetting quality and predictive performance. Evaluation Criteria. CONFIDENCE LEVEL AND CALIBRATION DATA In conformal prediction, miscoverage rate α and calibration set size are two crucial parameters for determining predic- tion set coverage and reliability. We next discuss the suitable settings for these two parameters and the rationale behind our chosen configuration. In terms of α, a higher confidence level (which is 1−α) pro- vides more reliable coverage but typically results in larger prediction sets. Common settings of confidence level are 0.95 and 0.9, corresponding to α values of 0.05 and 0.1, respectively. To make our work more broadly applicable and provide a comprehensive reference, we expand our ex- periments by setting α to a wider range of values: 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, and 0.2. Notably, our default and recommended value for α is 0.1 and subsequent experimental analysis is based on α = 0.1. Higher values of α would result in smaller, potentially more precise prediction sets, but this reduction comes at the cost of decreased confidence, which may not be acceptable in many applications. As for calibration data, it should be independent of train and test data. One requirement for the choice of the calibration set size is that the distribution of the calibration set should match the distribution of the test data as closely as possible. That means a small sample size may lead to distributional dissimilarity and unstable coverage estimation. Therefore, a sufficient sample size of calibration data must be ensured to obtain stable estimates. Figure 1 illustrates the stability of ˆq across varying calibration set sizes. We implement them on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18 in 10% and 50% random data forgetting scenarios. The results shown in Figure 1 are smoothed using B-spline. It reveals that 2, 000 is a sufficient calibration set size for different settings on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18 to get a stable threshold ˆq. Evaluating Unlearning Methods with New Metrics Having established the new metrics CR and MIACR, a nat- ural question to ask is: (Q3) Do existing machine unlearning methods truly achieve forgetting, and how do they perform under our new evaluation metrics? In this section, we assess the performance of various unlearn- ing methods using the newly introduced metrics, specifically CR, together with coverage and set size. We employ 9 dif- ferent unlearning methods, RT, FT (Warnecke et al., 2021), RL (Graves et al., 2021), Gradient Ascent (GA) (Thudi et al., 2022), Teacher (Tarun et al., 2023), FisherForget- ting (FF) (Golatkar et al., 2020a), SSD (Foster et al., 2024), NegGrad+ (Kurmanji et al., 2024) and Salun (Fan et al., 2023). The experimental results are presented in Table 4, which summarizes the unlearning performance under 10% random data forgetting scenario on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18. For more experimental results on CR and MIACR, please check Section 4 and Appendix B. The table 4 includes coverage percentages, set size, CR for both Df and Dtest, as well as ˆq in different settings of α. As observed, it shows a decreasing coverage and set size as the alpha increases in all methods since the threshold ˆq is relaxed due to the reduced confidence level. Based on evaluation criterion ➊, while NegGrad+ outper- forms RL under the traditional UA metric, RL exhibits su- perior performance under the CR metric. This observation suggests that methods excelling in traditional UA metric may not perform well under the CR metric. The underlying rationale behind this is that the CR metric takes into account the possibility that the true labels of some misclassified forget data points may still remain within the prediction set. This observation aligns with the insights we discussed in Section 2.2 regarding the limitation of UA. Based on evaluation criterion ➋, NegGrad+ and RL exhibit the best trade-off between forgetting quality and model performance. FF achieves the lowest CR, indicating the highest forgetting quality, but it exhibits the worst prediction performance on Dtest. On the other hand, GA, Teacher, SSD, FT and Salun maintain relatively high CR of the forget data Df across dif- ferent alpha settings, reflecting their poor forgetting quality. 3. Enhancing Machine Unlearning via Conformal Prediction Our analysis indicates that machine unlearning methods generally do not exhibit strong performance under our newly developed evaluation metrics. Even methods with relatively low CR values demonstrate significant compromises in other metrics. This observation raises an important question: (Q4) Can we explore advanced learning techniques via conformal prediction to optimize unlearning model’s performance under our evaluation metrics? 5 Conformal Prediction-Motivated Machine Unlearning A training-based machine unlearning method is typically op- timized for prediction loss but cannot efficiently support the improvement of forgetting quality in our new metrics. There- fore, we propose a novel and general unlearning framework for training-based machine unlearning methods to enhance machine unlearning. The key innovation of this framework lies in leveraging conformal prediction principles combined with a loss function inspired by the C&W attack (Carlini & Wagner, 2017) to improve forgetting quality. The original C&W loss function is designed to find adver- sarial examples that cause misclassification. Here we extend it to an unlearning loss. For forget data Df, the objective of the unlearning loss function is to decrease the model’s confidence in the true labels of Df. Based on this, the C&W-inspired unlearning loss can be defined as: Lcw(x, yt) = max  pt(x) −max i̸=t {pi(x)}, −∆  , (7) where (x, yt) ∈Df. pi(x) is the possibility (after softmax function) of class yi, while zt(x) is the true label yt’s pos- sibility output. We denote maxi̸=t{pi(x)} as the highest possibility value of the incorrect class. ∆is the margin parameter (also known as the confidence parameter) that controls the attack strength. This loss is minimized when pt(x)−maxi̸=t{pi(x)} ≤−∆ to make maxi̸=t{pi(x)}−pt(x) ≥∆. It means that the loss maximizes the difference between the highest possibility value for class yi (i ̸= t) and the possibility value for the true label yt, which makes it more difficult for the model to include the true label in the prediction set during conformal prediction process. Additionally, increasing the value of ∆further reduces the confidence of the true label yt being included in the prediction set. In our work, we set ∆= 0.01. Based on the insight discussed in Section 2, we further im- prove the C&W-inspired unlearning loss function by com- bining conformal prediction. In conformal prediction, cali- bration data helps in estimating non-conformity scores and determining a threshold to ensure valid statistical guaran- tees about the model’s uncertainty estimates. Therefore, we reserve a portion of calibration data D′ c for the unlearning phase, which is kept separate from the calibration data Dc used in the evaluation phase. According to Eq. 1, calibration data D′ c is used to calculate non-conformity scores and generate a threshold ¯q based on an α. Then, we calculate the non-conformity scores of Df to obtain the corresponding prediction set. Then, by revising C&W-inspired unlearning loss with this calibration step, a general unlearning loss function is defined as follows: Lunlearn(x, yt) = max (S(x, yt) −¯q, −∆) , (8) where (x, yt) ∈Df. We replace pt(x) in Eq. 7 with the non-conformity score S(x, yt) of true label yt, and replace maxi̸=t{pi(x)} with ¯q which will be updated before each epoch. It ensures that Lunlearn adheres to the principle of Lcw, which encourages ¯q −S(x, yt) ≥∆. It is a general framework applicable across various training- based machine unlearning methods. To preserve the effec- tiveness of specific machine unlearning methods, we retain their original loss Loriginal. Consequently, we sum these terms to form the final objective loss function as follows: Ltotal = Loriginal + λ · Lunlearn, (9) where λ is a hyperparameter that controls the forgetting degree. 4. Experiment 4.1. Experimental setting Datasets and Models. We report experiments on CIFAR- 10 (Krizhevsky, 2009) with ResNet-18 (He et al., 2016) and Tiny ImageNet (Le & Yang, 2015) with ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021). Implementation Details. For CIFAR-10/Tiny ImageNet, we randomly select 200/50 data points per class (2, 000/10, 000 data points in total) as calibration data Dc and D′ c, respectively. The calibration data Dc does not par- ticipate in the model training or unlearning processes and is only used for calibrating the threshold ˆq, while D′ c is used in the process of our unlearning framework to generate ¯q. For the hyperparameter in our work, miscoverage rate α ∈[0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2], margin parameter ∆= 0.01, un- learning loss weight λ ∈[0, 0.2, 0.5, 1]. Due to space lim- itations, more training details and experimental results under settings of α ∈[0.05, 0.15], λ = 0.2 and class- wise forgetting scenario can be found in Appendix A-C. 4.2. Measure Machine Unlearning Method via New Metrics CR Metric. For the CR metric, we already show the re- sults of CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18 in Tabel 4. On the contrary, the CR tends to increase with increasing α. Although both Cov- erage and Set Size may decrease, Set Size often decreases more significantly. Consequently, the CR value generally becomes larger as α increases. When α is set to 0.2, most methods show a value of Set Size less than 1 in both Table 4 and 5. The intuition behind it is that conformal prediction, as a static predictor, is in- trinsically tied to the model’s base prediction performance and accuracy. When the model’s accuracy is significantly higher than the confidence level, conformal prediction can achieve the required coverage with ease. In fact, it can gen- erate empty prediction sets for some data points while still meeting the target coverage. Thus, the choice of α is crucial. Overly high α values may skew evaluation results by failing to let CR accurately reflect model performance. Notably, when α = 0.2, RL’s coverage on the forget data Df decreases significantly compared to other methods. This re- sults from the use of label corruption during RL’s unlearning process, which enlarges the distribution difference between calibration data and forget data. We can mitigate this gap if we know the details of specific unlearning methods, and a potential solution to this issue is discussed in Appendix B. Regarding the forgetting quality of specific machine unlearn- ing methods, the Teacher method achieves the strongest performance on the traditional UA metric under both eval- uation criteria ➊and ➋. However, its forgetting quality is significantly weaker when measured by the CR metric. This highlights that the CR captures critical scenarios overlooked by UA, specifically the potential retention of true labels within prediction sets for the forget data points. By explic- itly addressing this phenomenon, CR ensures a more robust and reliable evaluation for unlearning quality. MIACR Metric. Related Work Machine unlearning has emerged as a vital research topic due to several privacy, regulatory, and ethical concerns as- sociated with machine learning models. It refers to the process of selectively removing specific data points from a trained machine-learning model. Generally, post-hoc ma- chine unlearning can be divided into training-based (Graves et al., 2021; Warnecke et al., 2021; Thudi et al., 2022; Tarun et al., 2023) and training-free approaches (Guo et al., 2019; Sekhari et al., 2021; Nguyen et al., 2020; Golatkar et al., 2020b; 2021; Foster et al., 2024). To evaluate these methods, several unlearning metrics have been proposed, including UA (Brophy & Lowd, 2021; Fos- ter et al., 2024) and MIA (Shokri et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021). However, these metrics often fail to account for the confidence of the forgetting quality. To address this limi- tation, we improve it in our work motivated by conformal prediction (Angelopoulos & Bates, 2021), which stands out among uncertainty quantification techniques for its ability to provide well-calibrated, reliable confidence measures. As a generic methodology, conformal prediction can trans- form the outputs of any black box prediction algorithm into a prediction set. Due to its versatility, many works have specifically designed numerous conformal prediction meth- ods tailored to particular prediction problems (Papadopoulos et al., 2002; Lei & Wasserman, 2014; Romano et al., 2020; Lei et al., 2018). One work (Becker & Liebig, 2022) has primarily focused on parameter-level uncertainty without fully addressing the broader implications of unlearning on prediction confidence. It assesses the sensitivity of model parameters to the target data through Fisher Information Matrix, but they often rely on computationally intensive operations and may struggle to scale to large models or datasets. 6. Conclusion Motivated by conformal prediction, we introduce new met- rics, CR and MIACR, to enhance the evaluation and reli- ability of machine unlearning. In addiction, our unlearn- ing framework, which incorporates the adapted C&W loss with conformal prediction, improves unlearning effective- ness. Together, we provide a more rigorous foundation for privacy-preserving machine learning. 8 Conformal Prediction-Motivated Machine Unlearning Impact Statement This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning. It looks like there is a significant discrepancy between the distribution of the forget data and the calibration data. To align the distribution of Dc with that of Df and minimize the differences between them, we design a shadow model. To make the explanation clearer and more intuitive, we take RL as an example. In the RL unlearning method, the forget data is assigned random labels. Therefore, we apply the same random labeling process to the calibration data and train a shadow model accordingly. We designed two methods: 1. Shadow model. A shadow model replicates the behavior of forget data Df throughout the unlearning process. A shadow model is a two-step approach: (1) it firstly trains a shadow original model θ′ o using train data Dtrain and clean calibration data Dc with the same epoch number as the original model θo; (2) subsequently, we finetune the θ′ o using the random labeled calibration data. 2. Semi-shadow model. The semi-shadow model only adopts the second step in the shadow model. It finetunes the original model θo with random-labeled calibration data. name of paper: Detection Is All You Need: A Feasible Optimal Prior-Free Black-Box Approach For Piecewise Stationary Bandits
summary: We study the problem of piecewise stationary bandits without prior knowledge of the underlying non-stationarity. We propose the first $\textit{feasible}$ black-box algorithm applicable to most common parametric bandit variants. Our procedure, termed Detection Augmented Bandit (DAB), is modular, accepting any stationary bandit algorithm as input and augmenting it with a change detector. DAB achieves optimal regret in the piecewise stationary setting under mild assumptions. Specifically, we prove that DAB attains the order-optimal regret bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{N_T T})$, where $N_T$ denotes the number of changes over the horizon $T$, if its input stationary bandit algorithm has order-optimal stationary regret guarantees. Applying DAB to different parametric bandit settings, we recover recent state-of-the-art results. Notably, for self-concordant bandits, DAB achieves optimal dynamic regret, while previous works obtain suboptimal bounds and require knowledge on the non-stationarity. In simulations on piecewise stationary environments, DAB outperforms existing approaches across varying number of changes. Interestingly, despite being theoretically designed for piecewise stationary environments, DAB is also effective in simulations in drifting environments, outperforming existing methods designed specifically for this scenario.

contents: Detection Is All You Need: A Feasible Optimal Prior-Free Black-Box Approach For Piecewise Stationary Bandits Argyrios Gerogiannis ag91@illinois.edu ECE and CSL, The Grainger College of Engineering University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign Urbana, IL 61801-2332, USA Yu-Han Huang yuhanhh2@illinois.edu ECE and CSL, The Grainger College of Engineering University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign Urbana, IL 61801-2332, USA Subhonmesh Bose boses@illinois.edu ECE and CSL, The Grainger College of Engineering University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign Urbana, IL 61801-2332, USA Venugopal V. Veeravalli vvv@illinois.edu ECE and CSL, The Grainger College of Engineering University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign Urbana, IL 61801-2332, USA Editor: N/A Abstract We study the problem of piecewise stationary bandits without prior knowledge of the underlying non- stationarity. We propose the first feasible black-box algorithm applicable to most common parametric bandit variants. Our procedure, termed Detection Augmented Bandit (DAB), is modular, accepting any stationary bandit algorithm as input and augmenting it with a change detector. DAB achieves optimal regret in the piecewise stationary setting under mild assumptions. Specifically, we prove that DAB at- tains the order-optimal regret bound of ˜O(√NT T), where NT denotes the number of changes over the horizon T, if its input stationary bandit algorithm has order-optimal stationary regret guarantees. Apply- ing DAB to different parametric bandit settings, we recover recent state-of-the-art results. Notably, for self-concordant bandits, DAB achieves optimal dynamic regret, while previous works obtain suboptimal bounds and require knowledge on the non-stationarity. In simulations on piecewise stationary environ- ments, DAB outperforms existing approaches across varying number of changes. Interestingly, despite being theoretically designed for piecewise stationary environments, DAB is also effective in simulations in drifting environments, outperforming existing methods designed specifically for this scenario. 1 Introduction Bandit environment models have found a variety of applications in engineering domains, e.g., in recom- mendation systems Li et al. (2010); Lefortier et al. (2014), online advertising Chapelle and Li (2011); Ser- tan et al. (2012); Schwartz et al. (2017), dynamic pricing Tajik et al. (2024) and real-time bidding Flajolet and Jaillet (2017). With its introduction via the multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem in Robbins (1952), a plethora of variants have now been studied. Parametric bandit (PB) problems in Auer (2002); Filippi et al. 1 arXiv:2501.19401v1 [cs.LG] 31 Jan 2025 (2010); Faury et al. (2020) define an important subclass, where an agent interacts with an environment over T rounds. At each round t, the agent chooses one action At among a set A ⊆Rd and receives a random reward, Xt = ft(At) + εt = µ (⟨θt, At⟩) + εt, where θt is an underlying governing parameter, unknown to the agent and µ : R →R is an injective function. Here, εt is a zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise. The agent seeks a causal control policy {πt}T t=1, where πt maps the history of actions and stochastic rewards up to time t −1 to an action At at time time t, to minimize the (dynamic) regret, RT := EAt∼πt " T X t=1 max a∈A ft(a) −ft(At) # . Bandit environments are often modeled as stationary, i.e., the reward distribution across actions re- main constant throughout (with θt’s being the same across time). However, this assumption rarely holds in practice; factors such as user preferences, product offerings, and market prices typically evolve over time. Non-stationarity is often categorized into two types–gradual drifts and abrupt changes. In the first cat- egory, the distributions change slowly with time, while in the latter, they shift suddenly and decisively at specific change-points. Such events can result from shifts in user behavior, emerging trends, competi- tive actions, etc. In this paper, we tackle the question of piecewise stationary parametric bandits (PS-PBs), where the reward distribution changes abruptly at times, 1 =: ν0 < ν1 < . . . < νNT < νNT +1 := T + 1. Thegoverningparametersθt’sthatdefinetherewarddistributionsatroundtstayconstantbetweenchange- points, i.e., θt = θt′ for rounds νk ≤t, t′ < νk+1, but change across each change-point, i.e., θνk−1 ̸= θνk. Here, NT defines the number of change-points over T rounds. The νk’s and NT are deemed un- known to the learner. The model we consider encompasses PS variants of linear bandits (LBs) with g as identity, general- ized linear bandits (GLBs), and self-concordant bandits (SCBs), where εt has a variance that depends on g (⟨θt, At⟩)andg hasacertainself-concordantproperty. ForPS-MABs,theminimax-optimal(information- theoretic) lower bound is ˜O(√NT T), ignoring problem-dependent constants Garivier and Moulines (2011).1 This result can be adapted to the PS-PB setting and establish the same lower bound. In this pa- per, we provide an algorithm which attains this lower bound under reasonable assumptions on minimal separations between the change-points. Such assumptions are mild, given that allowing change-points to occur in rapid succession violates the premise of piecewise stationarity, which requires sufficiently long stationary intervals between changes to enable algorithms to meaningfully respond to said changes. Algorithms for non-stationary (NS) bandits are either adaptive or restarting in nature. While adaptive methods continuously adjust the control policies in reaction to changes in reward distributions, restarting methods choose to unlearn and kickstart the learning process at certain times. When an algorithm relies on knowledge of the non-stationarity model, we call it prior-based. Otherwise, we call it prior-free. Discounted and sliding-window algorithms that weigh recent observations more heavily and forget the distant past are examples of prior-based adaptive approaches, e.g., see Kocsis and Szepesv´ari (2006); Garivier and Moulines (2011) for NS-MABs, Russac et al. (2019); Cheung et al. (2019); Wang et al. (2023) 1. We use ˜O(·) to suppress poly-logarithmic terms. 2 for NS-LBs, Russac et al. (2020); Faury et al. (2021); Wang et al. (2023) for NS-GLBs, and Russac et al. (2021); Wang et al. (2023) for NS-SCBs. The budget-restarting approaches in Besbes et al. (2014) for NS- MABs, Zhao et al. (2020) for NS-LBs, and Zhao et al. (2020) for NS-GLBs are examples of prior-based restarting algorithms. Finally, detection-based restarting algorithms come in both prior-based and prior- free forms. For NS-MABs, Liu et al. (2018); Cao et al. (2019) constitute such prior-based methods, while Auer et al. (2019); Besson et al. (2022); Huang et al. (2025) are examples of prior-free approaches. For NS-LBs, see Hong et al. (2023). In this paper, we propose and analyze a prior-free detection-based restarting method for PS-PBs. Our choice is motivated by the fact that prior knowledge of non-stationarity in practice is often unavailable and the observation that restarting methods have comparable or lower complexity than adaptive methods in worst-case scenarios, as shown in (Peng and Papadimitriou, 2024). Among prior-free algorithms, black-box approaches augment any stationary bandit algorithm to han- dle non-stationarity, instead of designing customized algorithms for the non-stationary setting. The MAS- TER algorithm in (Wei and Luo, 2021) provides the only known order-optimal black-box algorithm that applies to a very general class of reinforcement learning settings. In the recent work of (Gerogiannis et al., 2024), however, the authorsconclude thatthetheoreticallyoptimalMASTERalgorithmisnotquiteprac- tically feasible in that its non-stationarity detection mechanism does not get triggered for practical choices of the horizon (up to at least 1.24 billion), which in turn leads to performance issues. In this paper, we target a practical detection-restarting black-box algorithm that is tailored specifically for PS-PBs–a first of its kind to our knowledge. We provide a modular analysis for its regret upper bound that matches its minimax optimal lower bound up to log factors. To investigate our method’s behavior in different types of non-stationarity, we conduct experiments on piecewise stationary and drifting envi- ronments. Our results show that our approach significantly outperforms MASTER and state-of-the-art methods in the piecewise stationary setting. Surprisingly, it also excels in drifting environments, despite not being designed for them. To understand this, we offer an intuitive explanation for the conditions un- der which it can have good performance, which is validated through additional experiments in drifting settings. 1.1 Our Contributions • Wedesignapracticalprior-freedetection-basedrestartingblack-boxalgorithmthatattainsorder-optimal regret for PS-PBs, addressing an open problem. • We use change-detection using samples from forced exploration and combine that with a stationary bandit algorithm to handle PS settings. Our design is modular, easy to implement, and analyze. For PS- LBs and PS-GLBs, our regret bound matches state-of-art, while for PS-SCBs, we improve it significantly from Wang et al. (2023). • Our experiments on abruptly changing environments demonstrate that our approach significantly out- performs existing prior-free and prior-based methodologies. • Unexpectedly, our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in gradually changing environments, a setting it is not designed for. We provide intuition behind this observation and validate our hypothesis through additional experiments. 3 2 The Change Detection Mechanism Our restarting approach hinges on an effective mechanism to detect a change in the reward distributions–a premise that strongly correlates with good practical performance, according to Gerogiannis et al. (2024). The art lies in designing a detection mechanism that resets learning shortly after a change-point ν, but limits the probability of false alarm. Various detection tests have been proposed in the non-stationary bandit literature Liu et al. (2018); Cao et al. (2019); Auer et al. (2019); Besson et al. (2022); Hong et al. (2023);Huangetal.(2025). Weleverageachange-detectionmechanismthatalignswithBessonetal.(2022); Huang et al. (2025) and has strong ties to the long literature on quickest change detection, e.g., see Poor and Hadjiliadis (2009); Tartakovsky et al.(2014);Veeravalli andBanerjee(2013);Xie etal.(2021) forsurveys. To describe the change-detection procedure, consider the simplified bandit problem with a single change-point (NT = 1) and one action (A = {a}). Let ν denote the change point and define r0, r1, as ft(a) before and after ν, respectively, assuming |r0 −r1| ≥∆c > 0. Assume that the change occurs only after a pre-change window of length m, i.e., ν > m. A change detector D defines a causal stopping rule τ when a change is declared. Let Pν and Eν, respectively, represent the probability measure and the expectation, when the change-point occurs at ν. Define correspondingly, P∞and E∞, when there is no change. The latency ℓassociated with a stopping rule τ is the length of time post-change within which a change is declared with a probability 1 −δD, i.e., ℓ:= inf{t ∈[T] : Pν(τ ≥ν + t) ≤δD, ∀ν ∈[m + 1, T −t]}. Here, [a, b] = {a, a + 1, . . . , b} and [b] = [1, b] for two non-negative integers a < b. A good change detector D seeks to minimize ℓwith low false alarm probability over a finite horizon T, i.e., P∞(τ ≤T) ≤ δF, with δF ∈(0, 1). As our proof for the regret bound in Appendix A will reveal (see also Huang and Veeravalli (2025)), D must satisfy the following property to guarantee optimal regret growth rate. Property 1 D must satisfy ℓ, m ≲log T + log(1/δF) + log(1/δD). Consider the generalized likelihood ratio (GLR) test in Huang et al. (2025); Huang and Veeravalli (2025) with change detection stopping rule τ := inf {n ∈N : Gn ≥β (n, δF)}, where Gn := sup s∈[n] log sup η0∈R s Y i=1 pη0 (Xi) ! + log sup η1∈R n Y i=s+1 pη1 (Xi) ! −log sup η∈R n Y i=1 pη (Xi) ! , β (n, δF) := 6 log (1 + log (n)) + 5 2 log 4n3/2 δF ! + 11. in which pη is the density of a Gaussian random variable with mean η and variance σ2. According to Huang et al. (2025), the GLR test satisfies Property 1 when rewards have σ2-sub-Gaussian noise, even though the test statistic uses the Gaussian density. The statistic Gn admits the following closed-form ex- pression, Gn := sup s∈[n] s(ˆµ1:s −ˆµ1:n)2 2σ2 + (n −s)(ˆµs+1:n −ˆµ1:n)2 2σ2  where ˆµt:t′ is the empirical mean of samples {Xt, . . . , Xt′} for any t < t′ ∈N (see Huang et al. (2025); Kaufmann and Koolen (2021) for derivation). With such a change-detector D, we now present our detection-based restarting algorithm in the next section. 4 3 The DAB Algorithm In a stationary bandit environment, an effective algorithm should quickly focus on (near-)optimal actions to minimize regret. As a result, suboptimal actions are rarely selected. In a PS setting, however, changes may go undetected if they do not affect the actions the stationary bandit algorithm converges to. To iden- tify such changes, forced exploration of suboptimal actions is necessary. We achieve this in our detection augmented bandit (DAB) algorithm, formally presented in Algorithm 1, via selecting a ﬁnite subset of ac- tions, Ae = {ai : i ∈[da]} ⊆A, and playing them at a controlled frequency to balance between regret minimization and change detection.2 To maintain a modular framework for the PS-PB problem, we do not allow reward samples from forced exploration to influence the stationary bandit algorithm. However, allowing the change detector to use samples from bandit algorithm from all actions in A when |A| is finite, but only allowing forced exploration over actions in Ae improves empirical performance. We remark that this variation does not affect order-wise regret calculations, and employ this variation for our experiments. We force DAB to take actions in Ae for the first da time steps, where da = |Ae|, and follow the sta- tionary bandit algorithms for the next ⌈da/αk⌉−da time steps. That is, αk encodes the forced exploration frequency. We declare a change when any one among the da change detectors flags a change. Ae should be designed such that reward sequences associated with at least one action in Ae must exhibit an appreciable mean-shift with possible changes in θt’s. Suppose θt ∈Θ ⊂Rd. Define ∆c := inf θ̸=θ′∈Θ max a∈Ae |µ(⟨θ, a⟩) −µ(⟨θ′, a⟩)|. (1) Then, ∆c captures how well the actions in Ae can discern between candidate governing parameters in Θ. Theproofofourregretboundillustratesthat∆c cruciallyaffectstheperformanceofthechange-detectors. The more discernible the changes are, the easier the detection becomes. Since forced exploration incurs regret, Ae should ideally be chosen to minimize da while maximizing ∆c. If Θ and A are finite, one can solve (1) to construct Ae with the smallest da. If Θ contains vectors that span Rd, selecting d linearly independent actions with largest norms from A guarantees a non-zero ∆c. Our focus lies in prior-free algorithm design, and hence, we do not assume the knowledge of Θ, except possibly a norm bound, as commonly assumed in the literature (e.g., see Lattimore and Szepesv´ari (2020); Wei and Luo (2021)). Hence, the choice of Ae guided by the search for the largest number of linearly independent vectors in A with large norms is robust to variations in Θ. As such, this choice leads to |Ae| ≤d that guarantees order-optimal regret from DAB in Section 4. 4 Performance Analysis of DAB TocharacterizeDAB’sperformance, wedevelopamodularregretupperboundbyincorporatingtheregret analysis of the stationary bandit algorithm and the latency of the change detector. Let RB be the regret upper bound of the stationary bandit algorithm B. In addition, let ℓD and mD be the latency and the pre- change window length of the change detector D. Moreover, as emphasized in Section 1, we assume that νk −νk−1 should be large enough so that the change detector will be triggered and DAB will restart before the next change occurs. Finally, without loss of generality, we assume that3 maxa′∈A ft(a′) −ft(a) ≤C for all a ∈A and t ∈[T]. The agent is unaware of C. The following result provides the regret upper bound. 2. We use ai to denote the i-th action in Ae. 3. Assuming such an upper bound is reasonable, since without such a bound, the (worst-case) regret could potentially be infi- nite. 5 Algorithm 1 Detection Augmented Bandit (DAB) Input: B, D, T, A, Ae, {αk}∞ k=1 Initialization: da ←|Ae|, τ ←0, Ha,D ←∅∀a ∈Ae, HB ←∅, k ←1 1: for t = 1, 2, . . . , T do 2: if (t −τ −1) mod ⌈da/αk⌉+ 1 = i ≤da then 3: At ←ai 4: Play action At and receive the reward Xt 5: HAt,D ←HAt,D ∪{Xt} 6: if D (HAt,D) = True then 7: τ ←t 8: ∀a ∈Ae, Ha,D ←∅ 9: HB ←∅ 10: k ←k + 1 11: end if 12: else 13: At ←B (HB) 14: Play action At and receive the reward Xt 15: HB ←HB ∪{(Xt, At)} 16: end if 17: end for Theorem 1 Assume the problem setting of Section 1. Consider Algorithm 1, using a change detector D with parameters δF and δD, a stationary bandit algorithm B, and forced exploration frequencies (αk)NT +1 k=1 . Suppose that ν1 ≥⌈da/αk⌉mD and νk −νk−1 ≥⌈da/αk−1⌉ℓD + ⌈da/αk⌉mD for k ∈[2, NT ]. Then, for suﬃciently large T, the regret is upper bounded as follows: RT ≤CTda(NT + 1)δF + CTNT δD + C NT X k=1 ⌈da/αk⌉ℓD + (NT + 1)RB  T NT + 1  + C[¯αT + (NT + 1)da] (2) where ¯α := maxk=1,...,NT +1 αk. Furthermore, if RB(T) = ˜O(dp√ T) with p ≥0.5, δF = δD = T −γ for γ > 1, and αk = α0 p kda log (T) /T, then RT = ˜O(dpp NT T). While the general regret upper bound in (2) appears to be linear in T, the later part of the result confirms the order-optimal sublinear growth in regret with appropriate choices for δF, δD, and {αk}. We explain the terms in our upper bound of (2) in the order of appearance. The first term arises from false alarms, where NT + 1 is the number of intervals, each with false alarm probability δF, leading to linear regret CT per event. The second term accounts for late detections, where NT change points each have a detection failure probability δD, also incurring CT regret per event. The third term captures regret due to detection delays. The fourth term results from the stationary bandit algorithm, with regret maximized when interval lengths are evenly distributed as T/(NT + 1). We remark that the variance of the noise εt in SCB is depen- dent on the mean reward itself. In particular, Var[εt | At] = ˙µ(⟨θt, At⟩). Many environments in practice drift slowly over time. DAB is not designed to handle drifting non-stationarity; in fact, a drifting non-stationary environment can be viewed as a PS environment with no lower bound on the length of the stationary intervals. Therefore, one might expect DAB to perform poorly for such environments compared to those algorithms which are specifically de- signed to handle said nature of non-stationary. In what follows, we first present the counterintuitive result that DAB outperformed other algorithms even in the drifting setup, and then proceed to investigate why and when this happens. To compare DAB with other algorithms, we adopted the following drift model: in each run, θt was changed linearly over T rounds from θinit to θfinal as θt = (1 −t/T) · θinit + (t/T) · θfinal, where these end-points were chosen the same way as described in Section 5.1. The noise and reward struc- tures were deemed identical to those in Section 5.1. The performance comparisons for drifting LB, GLB, and SCB are presented in Figure 4. ADA-OPKB proved to result in much larger cumulative regret com- pared to other algorithms. Being non-competitive, we omitted its performance from Figure 4. Based on ourplots, DABsignificantlyoutperformedothermethodsinthedriftingenvironment. Infact, itfaredbet- ter than the WeightUCB method from Wang et al. (2023), which not only is known to attain the optimal regret bound in the drifting setup, but has also been shown to perform well in practice. Our last set of results naturally lead us to ask when and why does DAB perform well in drifting envi- ronments. As a first step to study this question, we performed another experiment with LBs. We allowed the governing parameter θt in each time-step to evolve randomly as follows. At time t, we chose θt+1 := θt + ζt+1 where ζt+1 ∈Rd was chosen uniformly over a δ-ball. If the resulting θt+1 violated the norm-bound on Θ, we disregarded that choice of ζt+1 and sampled again. We repeated the process till it satisfied the norm- bound. We sampled εt ∼N(0, 0.1) at each t. We compared the cumulative dynamic regret up to time T of DAB+LinUCB and WeightUCB for a range of δ’s in Figure 5. The remaining parameters were chosen the same as those in Section 5.1. The DAB algorithm performed better than WeightUCB for smaller values of δ, but the conclusion reversed upon increasing δ. We now shed light into our hypothesis behind the observations from Figure 5. For playing an action a ∈A at time t + 1, we get the random reward, Xt+1 = ⟨θt, a⟩+ ⟨ζt+1, a⟩+ εt+1. (3) If the governing parameter did not change, then the corresponding reward from playing action a would have been X′ t+1 = ⟨θt, a⟩+ ε′ t+1, where ε′ t+1 is another realization of the noise. Statistically, a specific instance of ⟨ζt+1, a⟩+ εt+1 and ε′ t+1 are close to each other, when δ is small, albeit the resulting (small) mean-shift due to the drift in the governing parameter. For practical purposes, the impact of the drift can be absorbed into the noise term εt+1 when δ is small. As a result, one expects an algorithm tailored to handle piecewise stationarity to perform reasonably well for slowly drifting environments. On the other hand, if δ is large, the bias induced by ζt+1 is large enough to disallow absorbing it into the zero-mean noise term. Over a few time-steps, the cumulative effect of this compounding bias is then large enough to completely violate the stationarity assumption. As a result, DAB should not perform well, whereas algorithms designed specifically for drifting non-stationarity should achieve better performance. 6 Summary and Outlook In this work, we introduce DAB, the first practically feasible, prior-free, order-optimal black-box approach for piecewise stationary bandits. Designed for piecewise parametric bandit variants, DAB achieves order- optimal regret if its input stationary bandit algorithm has order-optimal stationary regret guarantees. The modularity of DAB makes it both theoretically analyzable and easy to implement with various stationary bandit algorithms. Crucially, DAB preserves and adapts the regret properties of its stationary input algo- rithm to the piecewise-stationary setting. As a result, it matches the best existing bounds in PS-LBs and PS-GLBs while significantly improving the best known bound for PS-SCBs. To evaluate its practical performance, we tested DAB in both piecewise stationary and drifting en- vironments. In the piecewise stationary setting, DAB dominates the prior-free black-box gold standard, MASTER, as well as state-of-the-art prior-based and prior-free methods. Even more strikingly, despite not being designed for drifting environments, DAB still outperforms the best known prior-based method, WeightUCB, along with MASTER and other prior-free approaches. To explain these unexpected results, we hypothesized key conditions under which DAB excels–an insight further validated through additional experiments under drifting settings. Our results reinforce a key insight from Gerogiannis et al. (2024): effective non-stationarity detection is critical for strong practical performance. Moreover, they suggest that a well-designed algorithm for the piecewise stationary setting can extend to a broad range of drifting scenarios, bridging the gap between these two regimes. This opens intriguing research directions in more general non-stationary bandit and 12 reinforcementlearningproblems, wherestudyingpiecewisestationaritycouldaddressasignificantportion of the challenge. Finally, DAB’s modular design invites future exploration into its extension across all piecewise stationary bandit settings, with the goal of achieving order-optimal bounds across the board. name of paper: A note on spontaneous symmetry breaking in the mean-field Bose gas
summary: We consider the homogeneous mean-field Bose gas at positive temperature. We show that spontaneous $U(1)$ symmetry breaking occurs if and only if the system displays Bose-Einstein condensation in the sense that the one-particle density matrix of the Gibbs state has a macroscopic eigenvalue.

Introduction and main results 1.1. Spontaneous symmetry breaking and quasi-averages Spontaneous symmetry breaking plays a pivotal role in understanding complex phenomena across various domains of physics, from condensed matter systems to high-energy particle interactions. Generally, it refers 1 to a situation when a symmetry of the Hamiltonian or Lagrangian of a system is not present in the state under consideration - usually a ground state or a thermal equilibrium state. In this note, we shall investigate symmetry breaking in a system of weakly interacting bosons. In non- relativistic quantum many-body systems, the associated symmetry is the U(1) symmetry corresponding to particle number conservation of the underlying many-body Hamiltonian (cf. (1.8)). It is a paradigm of statistical physics that phase transitions are accompanied by symmetry breaking. Since the seminal papers of Bose and Einstein [8, 18] it is known that the ideal (non-interacting) Bose gas undergoes a phase transition called the Bose-Einstein Condensation (BEC) phase transition (cf. Sections 1.4 and 1.5 for a brief reminder). It is characterized by a macroscopic occupation of a single quantum state and has been ﬁrst observed in experiments led by Ketterle, Cornell and Wieman [12, 23]. Mathematically, this has been shown to be true for interacting systems in various scaling regimes, in particular in the so-called mean-ﬁeld scaling. The main result of this paper shows that the BEC phase transition in the mean-ﬁeld Bose gas is indeed equivalent to the breaking of the U(1) symmetry of the underlying many-body system. While the deﬁnition of Bose-Einstein condensation (cf. (1.16)) is rather simple, a mathematically rigorous description of symmetry breaking is a bit more subtle. In order to explain it, let us focus on a translation- invariant system. In this case, the macroscopically occupied single particle quantum state in the condensed phase corresponds to the zero momentum mode, i.e. the expected number of particles with zero momentum ⟨a∗ 0a0⟩(cf. (1.5) and (1.6) for a deﬁnition of creation and annihilation operators) becomes proportional to the total number of particles in the system. This makes the zero momentum mode the most relevant one and, as suggested by Bogoliubov [5], justiﬁes to treat them classically by replacing the operators a0 and a∗ 0 by c-numbers and thus equating ⟨a∗ 0a0⟩and |⟨a0⟩|2. As the latter quantity cannot be non-zero in any state that has a ﬁxed number of particles, it serves as a marker of spontaneous symmetry breaking. In order to mathematically implement those ideas, Bogoliubov [6, 7] designed a limiting procedure that nowadays goes under the name of Bogoliubov’s quasi averages and has found applications in various ﬁelds of physics. It consists of the following two steps. First, in order to make the expectation value of a0 possibly non-zero, one adds to the many-body Hamiltonian a perturbation λ √ V(a∗ 0 + a0) that breaks particle number conservation (here V is the volume of the system). Let us denote by ⟨·⟩λ the expectation value in such a perturbed state. One then considers the double limit lim λ→0 lim V→∞ |⟨a0⟩λ|2 V and says that a non-zero value means that the symmetry is broken in the system. We stress the order of limits, which means that one ﬁrst takes the macroscopic limit and only later ’removes’ the symmetry breaking pertur- bation. Here, we also assume the macroscopic limit to be the thermodynamic limit, as originally considered by Bogoliubov. Note that the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality implies that |⟨a0⟩λ|2 V ≤ ⟨a∗ 0a0⟩λ V and thus spontaneous symmetry breaking implies BEC in the sense of quasi averages. In 2005 Lieb, Seiringer and Yngvason in [28], and, independently, Süt˝o in [39] proved that those two are in fact equivalent. Those works were inspired by the result of Ginibre [20] which gave the ﬁrst rigorous justiﬁcation of the c-number substitution. In [28] the authors have also shown that if there is BEC in the usual sense, then there is sponta- neous symmetry breaking, i.e. lim V→∞ ⟨a∗ 0a0⟩λ=0 V ≤lim λ→0 lim V→∞ |⟨a0⟩λ|2 V (1.1) Let us stress that all these statements are conditional in the sense that proving BEC in the thermodynamic limit remains a major open problem in mathematical physics. 2 While the problem in the thermodynamic limit remains open, one can ask the same question in other scaling regimes that are easier to handle. To this end, as already mentioned, we will consider the so-called mean-ﬁeld scaling (cf. (1.8) which corresponds to the physical situation of a weakly interacting gas. The zero temperature properties of this model are rather well understood: the ground state exhibits BEC [9, 24, 30] while excited states are well described by Bogoliubov theory [13, 21, 25, 33, 38]. At positive temperatures, an exhaustive description of the Gibbs state of the (translation invariant) mean-ﬁeld Bose gas has been given in [14]. See also [17, Section 1.6] for a discussion of the accuracy of Hartree theory in the trapped system. The remaining part of the introduction will be devoted to a detailed description of the model and a precise formulation of the main results. Notation We write a ≲b to say that there exists a constant C > 0 independent of the relevant parameters (for instance, the particle number or the inverse temperature) such that a ≤Cb holds. If a ≲b and b ≲a we write a ∼b, and a ≃b means that the leading orders of a and b are equal in the limit considered. In case the constant depends on a parameter k, we write a ≲k b and a ∼k b. 1.2. Bosonic Fock space and Hamiltonian We consider a system of bosonic particles conﬁned to the three-dimensional ﬂat torus Λ. The one-particle Hilbert space of the system is given by L2(Λ). We are interested in the grand canonical ensemble, that is, in systems with a ﬂuctuating particle number. The Hilbert space of the entire system is therefore given by the bosonic Fock space F(L2(Λ)) = ∞ M n=0 L2 sym(Λn) (1.2) over L2(Λ). Here, L2 sym(Λn) denotes the closed linear subspace of L2(Λn) consisting of those functions Ψ(x1, ..., xn) that are invariant under any permutation of the particle coordinates x1, ..., xn ∈Λ. Moreover, L2 sym(Λ0) = C. On the n-particle Hilbert space L2 sym(Λn) we deﬁne the Hamiltonian Hn η = n X i=1 −∆i + 1 η X 1≤i<j≤n v(d(xi, xj)). (1.3) Here ∆i denotes the Laplace-Beltrami operator acting on the coordinate xi and represents the kinetic energy of the particles. In the representation of the unit torus as the set [0, 1]3, ∆is the usual Laplacian with periodic boundary conditions. Moreover, d(·, ·) denotes the distance on the torus and the function v : R+ →R+ describes the interaction between the particles. The parameter η > 0 will later be shown (cf. Proposition 1.1) to be proportional to the expected number of particles in the system. That is, it implements a mean-ﬁeld scaling. The Hamiltonian of the entire system acts on a suitable dense subset of F(L2(Λ)) and is deﬁned by Hη = ∞ M n=0 Hn η. (1.4) To state an alternative representation of this Hamiltonian, we introduce the creation and annihilation oper- ators a∗ p and ap of a particle in the one-particle function ϕp(x) = eip·x with p ∈Λ∗= 2πZ3. The annihilation operator ap is a map from L2 sym(Λn) to L2 sym(Λn−1) for n ≥1 that satisﬁes apΩ= 0 for Ω= (1, 0, 0, ...) ∈F. Its action on an n-particle function ψ ∈L2 sym(Λn) is deﬁned by (apψ)(x1, ..., xn−1) = √n Z Λ e−ip·xψ(x1, ..., xn−1, x) dx, (1.5) 3 and for general ψ ∈F this action is extended by linearity. The creation operator a∗ p is the adjoint of ap and acts on ψ ∈L2 sym(Λn) as (a∗ pψ)(x1, ..., xn+1) = √ n + 1 n X j=1 eip·xjψ(x1, ..., xj−1, xj+1, ..., xn). (1.6) The above family of operators satisﬁes the canonical commutation relations [ap, a∗ q] = δp,q, [ap, aq] = 0 = [a∗ p, a∗ q]. (1.7) An alternative representation of the Hamiltonian in (1.4) in terms of these operators is given by Hη = X p∈Λ∗ p2a∗ pap + 1 2η X p,u,v∈Λ∗ ˆv(p)a∗ u+pa∗ v−pauav (1.8) with the Fourier coeﬃcients ˆv(p) = R Λ v(|x|)e−ip·x dx of the interaction potential v. 1.3. The grand canonical ensemble We are interested in a bosonic many-particle system described by the grand canonical ensemble. The usual parameters of this ensemble1 are the inverse temperature β > 0 and the chemical potential µ ∈R. The choice of the latter allows one to obtain any desired value for the expected number of particles N(β, µ) > 0 in the system. This, in particular, allows us to ensure the interpretation of the mean-ﬁeld scaling as in the canonical setup. The set of states on the bosonic Fock space is given by S = {Γ ∈B(F) | 0 ≤Γ, Tr Γ = 1} , (1.9) where B(F) denotes the set of bounded operators on F(L2(Λ)). For a state Γ ∈S the grand potential functional G is deﬁned by G(Γ) = Tr[(Hη −µN)Γ] −1 βS (Γ) with the von-Neumann entropy S (Γ) = −Tr[Γ ln(Γ)]. (1.10) Here µ ∈R and N = ∞ M n=0 n = X p∈Λ∗ a∗ pap (1.11) denote the chemical potential and the number operator, respectively. Its minimum equals the grand potential Φ(β, µ) = min Γ∈S G(Γ) = −1 β ln  Tr exp(−β(Hη −µN))  (1.12) and the unique minimizer of G in the set S is the grand canonical Gibbs state Gβ,µ = exp  −β(Hη −µN)  Tr exp  −β(Hη −µN) . (1.13) The expected number of particles in the Gibbs state Gβ,µ will be denoted by N(β, µ), that is N(β, µ) = Tr[NGβ,µ]. (1.14) 1A third parameter is the volume of the torus. Since there is a free parameter in our model, we decided to set it equal to one. 4 1.4. One-particle reduced density matrix and Bose–Einstein condensation Let Γ ∈S be a state for which NΓ is trace class. We deﬁne the one-particle density matrix (1-pdm) γΓ ∈ B(L2(Λ)) of Γ via its integral kernel in Fourier space by γΓ(p, q) = Tr[a∗ qapΓ]. (1.15) It is a nonnegative trace-class operator, which satisﬁes tr[γΓ] = Tr[NΓ]. Following [36] we say that a sequence of states ΓN ∈S with Tr[NΓN] = N displays Bose–Einstein condensation (BEC) iﬀ lim inf N→∞sup ∥ψ∥=1 ⟨ψ, γΓNψ⟩ N > 0, (1.16) that is, iﬀthe largest eigenvalue of γΓN growths proportionally to N. The largest eigenvalue of γΓN divided by N and the corresponding eigenvector are called the condensate fraction and the condensate wave function, respectively. Organization of the article and strategy of proof The proofs of both main results, Proposition 1.1 and Theorem 1.1, are based on a variational approach. In Section 2 we provide upper and lower bounds for the grand potential related to the unperturbed Hamil- tonian. The proof of the upper bound relies on a trial state that treats the zero momentum mode as a coherent state and the excited particles as those of an ideal gas with an appropriately chosen chemical potential. The lower bound is a straightforward consequence of the Onsager Lemma 2.1. The proof of Theorem 1.1 is divided into several steps. First in Section 3, we provide upper and lower bounds for the grand potential of the perturbed Hamiltonian (1.22). In fact, apart from the the symmetry breaking perturbation, we need to consider also another perturbation of the form δa∗ 0a0. The upper bound uses a similar trial state as the one used for the non-perturbed Hamiltonian. However, now, the condensate part of the trial state has to take into account the right phase - as induced by the symmetry breaking term. The lower bound is more involved and, in the ﬁrst step, uses the Onsager Lemma and a c-number substitution. Using entropic inequalities in the spirit of [16] (cf. Section 3.2) one then arrives at an expression which can be minimized using perturbation theory. The bounds on the perturbed grand potential are used in Section 4 to give the proof of Theorem 1.1. To obtain information on the quasi-average in (1.29), one diﬀerentiates the grand potential of the system with respect to λ. Since it is a concave function of λ, one can apply a Griﬃth (Hellmann–Feynman) argument to obtain bounds on the quasi-averages from bounds on the grand potential. This, however, only yields bounds for the expectation of a0 + a∗ 0 in the perturbed Gibbs state. To conclude the desired statement, one has to combine these estimates with (1.30), which can again be proved with a Griﬀth (Hellmann–Feynman) argument. Finally, Appendix A is devoted to the analysis of the equation (1.23) and the derivation of the basic proper- ties of the eﬀective chemical potential. 2. name of paper: The Gibbs state of the mean-field Bose gas
summary: We consider the homogeneous mean-field Bose gas at temperatures proportional to the critical temperature of its Bose--Einstein condensation phase transition. Our main result is a trace-norm approximation of the grand canonical Gibbs state in terms of a reference state, which is given by a convex combination of products of coherent states and Gibbs states associated with certain temperature-dependent Bogoliubov Hamiltonians. The convex combination is expressed as an integral over a Gibbs distribution of a one-mode $\Phi^4$-theory describing the condensate. We interpret this result as a justification of Bogoliubov theory at positive temperature. Further results derived from the norm approximation include various limiting distributions for the number of particles in the condensate, as well as precise formulas for the one- and two-particle density matrices of the Gibbs state. Key ingredients of our proof, which are of independent interest, include two novel abstract correlation inequalities. The proof of one of them is based on an application of an infinite-dimensional version of Stahl's theorem.

Properties of the effective chemical potential 90 C. Properties of the ideal Bose gas 92 D. Bounds related to a perturbed Bogoliubov Hamiltonian 94 1. Introduction and main results 1.1. Background and summary The theory of Bose gases began about a hundred years ago with the introduction of Bose–Einstein statistics in the pioneering works of Bose and Einstein [23, 45]. Based on their analysis of the ideal (non-interacting) gas, they predicted the condensation of a macroscopic number of particles into a single quantum state (Bose– Einstein condensation (BEC)), a phenomenon that was also conjectured to occur in interacting bosonic many- particle systems at suﬃciently low temperatures. In 1947, Bogoliubov [21] realized that the occurrence of BEC in such systems allows one, at least formally, to replace certain operators in the Hamiltonian associated with the condensate by complex numbers (the so-called c-number substitution). By additionally neglecting 2 terms in the Hamiltonian that are expected to be small, one obtains an explicitly solvable model. This model predicts that the low-energy excitations of the Hamiltonian are sound waves, which implies superﬂuid behav- ior of the system (ﬂow without friction). These considerations are now collectively referred to as Bogoliubov theory. The proof of Bose–Einstein condensation (BEC) and the justiﬁcation of Bogoliubov’s theory from micro- scopic principles in various parameter regimes remain major challenges in modern mathematical physics. In 2002 a proof of BEC was obtained by Lieb and Seiringer [72] in the Gross–Pitaevskii limit, which is a scaling regime used to describe dilute trapped Bose gases. Moreover, in the breakthrough article [17], Boccato, Bren- necke, Cenatiempo, and Schlein recently demonstrated that in the same limit Bogoliubov theory correctly predicts the low-lying excitation spectrum of a dilute Bose gas. Shortly afterward, the Lee–Huang–Yang for- mula [64] for the ground-state energy (zero-temperature case) of the dilute Bose gas in the more challenging thermodynamic limit was established by Fournais and Solovej in [49, 50]. Their work conﬁrmed the pre- dictions of Bogoliubov theory in this setting and concluded a series of remarkable contributions made over the last 65 years [6, 8, 31, 43, 46, 52, 78, 104]. A related conjecture for the free energy at low temperatures, where the entropy is proportional to the contribution of the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum, has been proved recently in [54,55]. Some earlier results on the free energy of the dilute Bose gas in the thermodynamic limit can be found in [39,79,97,105]. Despite this impressive progress, a proof of the Bose–Einstein condensation phase transition in the thermo- dynamic limit appears to be beyond the reach of current mathematical techniques, let alone a detailed study of the properties of the Gibbs state. However, see [5] for an overview of an ambitious long-term project aimed at proving BEC in the thermodynamic limit with renormalization group techniques. From a conceptual perspec- tive, the thermodynamic limit is diﬃcult to analyze because the kinetic energy operator looses its spectral gap, which prevents the use of coercivity of the relevant energy functionals to extract information about the states. In particular, it remains unclear, even heuristically, when Bogoliubov theory breaks down and what types of corrections should be expected. In the present paper, we study the Gibbs state of the homogeneous Bose gas in the mean-ﬁeld limit. This parameter regime is easier to analyze than the thermodynamic limit but still exhibits a rich mathematical structure. For this model, BEC and the validity of Bogoliubov theory for the low-lying excitation spectrum were established in Seiringer’s seminal paper [98]. His proof inspired much of the later work on the subject and laid the basis for our current understanding of Bogoliubov theory, which eventually led to a proof of the Lee–Huang–Yang formula. When the interaction, temperature, and chemical potential of the model are chosen such that the system approaches the critical point of the BEC phase transition from above, Bogoliubov theory becomes inapplicable. As shown independently by Lewin, Nam, and Rougerie in [67] and by Fr¨ohlich, Knowles, Schlein, and Sohinger in [51], the correct description of the system in this parameter regime is given by a nonlinear classical ﬁeld theory. Observing these eﬀects requires a stronger interaction than that considered in Seiringer’s work. The existing results on the mean-ﬁeld Bose gas do not provide information about the Gibbs state at temper- atures comparable to the critical temperature for BEC, where the phase transition from the condensed to the non-condensed phase can be observed. The aim of the present paper is to address this question. We prove that the Gibbs state of the interacting model can be eﬃciently described by a convex combination of products of co- herent states and Gibbs states associated with certain temperature-dependent Bogoliubov Hamiltonians. This convex combination is expressed as an integral over a Gibbs distribution of a one-mode Φ4-theory describing the condensate, recently introduced by Boccato, Deuchert, and Stocker in [20]. Justifying this approximation requires the development of general techniques that go substantially beyond the use of coercivity of the Gibbs free energy functional. More precisely, while we start with a variational formulation of the problem, the ap- plication of two new abstract correlation inequalities allows us to derive results for the Gibbs state that are not shared by approximate minimizers of the energy functional. We expect that the general tools developed in this paper are of independent interest and will pave the way toward a better understanding of the Bose gas 3 at positive temperature in other scaling regimes as well. Other main results, derived from our norm approxi- mation of the Gibbs state and the application of our new correlation inequalities, include the computation of the various limiting distributions for the number of particles in the condensate, precise formulas for the one- and two-particle density matrices of the Gibbs state, as well as an asymptotic expansion of the free energy. In the following, we introduce our model and highlight a few key results and ideas. Other main results, which require more notation to be stated, will be presented in Section 2. Notation We write a ≲b to say that there exists a constant C > 0 independent of the relevant parameters (for instance, the particle number or the inverse temperature) such that a ≤Cb holds. If a ≲b and b ≲a we write a ∼b, and a ≃b means that the leading orders of a and b are equal in the limit considered. In case the constant depends on a parameter k, we write a ≲k b and a ∼k b. By ∥· ∥p we denote the standard Lp-norm. We understand all traces of the form Tr[AΓ] with a positive operator A and a positive trace-class operator Γ in the sense of quadratic forms. That is, we deﬁne Tr[AΓ] ≔Tr[Γ1/2AΓ1/2]. This expression is always well-deﬁned if one allows the value +∞. The many-body quantum model We consider a system of bosonic particles conﬁned to the torus Λ = [0, 1]3. The one-particle Hilbert space is given by L2(Λ). So far, the existing studies in the mean-ﬁeld regime mostly focused on the ground state problem or the Gibbs state at temperature of order 1. In these cases, most particles occupy the condensate, and only a ﬁnite number of particles remains in the thermal cloud; see [80, 84] for a robust justiﬁcation of this fact with exponential estimates. Coherent states and Bogoliubov theory Unlike the ideal gas, the interacting Bose gas is not exactly solvable. In fact, the presence of interactions gives rise to intriguing quantum phenomena, whose understanding is, in general, mathematically very challenging. A cornerstone of the theory of interacting Bose gases is Bogoliubov’s seminal paper [21], in which he intro- duced an eﬀective, explicitly solvable model (the Bogoliubov Hamiltonian) to explain superﬂuidity in such system. The main idea proposed by Bogoliubov is to replace a0 and a∗ 0 in the Hamiltonian of a system in the condensed phase with a complex number, whose absolute value is proportional to pTr[a∗ 0a0Gβ,N] ≫1. A rigorous way to implement this ideas is the c-number substitution using coherent states [60, 75], which we now explain in more detail. We start by considering the case of zero temperature. Let us now come to the discussion of the positive temperature case, which is the main concern of the present paper. 7 Positive temperature We introduce a positive temperature to the system that is proportional to the critical temperature of the BEC phase transition. In this case we can encounter a situation, where Tr[a∗ 0a0Gβ,N] ∼N (order N condensed particles) and N −Tr[a∗ 0a0Gβ,N] ∼N (order N particles are thermally excited). Following an idea that has been proposed by Lee, Huang, and Yang in 1958 [65] we note that for typical eigenstates of the Hamiltonian, we expect to have |z|2 ≃Tr[a∗ 0a0Gβ,N]. Thus, this part of the c-number substitution clearly continues to make sense. However, one crucial assumption of Bogoliubov theory is violated in the positive temperature setting: namely, that all terms in the Hamiltonian involving no or only one factor of z or z are small. In fact, it is not diﬃcult to see that some of these terms are of order N and, therefore, contribute to the leading order of the interaction energy. This relates to a question raised in the physics literature about the temperature at which the validity of Bogoliubov theory breaks down; see, e.g., [2]. A key insight in our work is that Bogoliubov theory remains valid in the presence of a macroscopic number of thermally excited particles, as long as the temperature stays on the order of the critical temperature. The reason is that the interaction terms, which can be neglected at zero temperature, do not alter the structure of the Gibbs state. For some terms, this is due to their particular form (in the case of density-density interactions), while for others, it is because they are small enough. Proving these claims requires a delicate analysis of the properties of the interacting Gibbs state, which constitutes the main contribution of the present article. A key ingredient for this analysis is our new set of abstract correlation inequalities. We emphasize that some terms in the Hamiltonian are small only when expectations are taken with respect to the Gibbs state. (a) Since each term in the Hamiltonian HN in (1.7) consists of an even number of creation and annihilation operators the Gibbs state Gβ,N satisﬁes [Gβ,N, N] = 0. Here, a pure phase is represented by a state in which each z appearing in the integration has a ﬁxed phase. (c) The function gBEC describes the particle number ﬂuctuations of the condensate. As we will see later, its variance is of the order N5/3 if N0(β, N) ≳N5/6.
